To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the radio continuum emission from deeply embedded protostars is a powerful tool to study the physical properties of low luminosity sources.
we have detected a sample of deeply embedded young protellar regions, and have determined their 1.8cm radio luminosity to total luminosity correlation.
We have detected and identified 15 compact radio sources towards 13 Spitzer c2dc2d small clouds & cores regions at 1.8cm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the earliest phases of low mass star formation and the detection of radio continuum emission from deeply embedded protostellar sources.
the physical properties of low luminosity young stellar objects (YSOs) in the early stages of their formation.
the physical conditions in the immediate vicinity of protostars, the ionizing sources, the ionized gas and the magnetic field, and the role of radio observations in understanding these conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the radio emission from young protostars is dominated by free‐free emission from ionized gas, but that a contribution from thermal bremsstrahlung cannot be ruled out.
the cm‐wave continuum emission from deeply embedded low luminosity protoplanetary systems can be explained by a combination of free–free emission and synchrotron emission.
we are still a long way from understanding the nature of the cm‐wave radio emission from deeply embedded protostellar objects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the radio continuum emission is a good probe for the deeply embedded protostars in low luminosity regions.
radio continuum observations at cm‐waves are useful tools for the study of the earliest stages of low‐mass star formation.
the radio luminosity is a useful probe of protostellar luminosity and that radio emission can be detected from low luminosity protoclusters and individual protostars.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cm‐wave radio continuum emission from low luminosity protobinary stars can be detected and measured with current radio facilities and that the emission can be used to constrain their internal luminosity and hence their evolutionary stage.
the cm‐wave radio emission is a useful tool for studying the internal structure of low luminosity objects.
the 1.2 cm and 1.8cm radio continuum emission from deeply embedded protostars can be used to probe their internal luminosities, and hence their accretion rates, even at the very lowest luminosities.
